questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that an architect's job is not to maximize every NFR category at once?
options: Because NFRs compete for the same finite budget of time, money, and architectural complexity, and improving one often degrades another, so the real job is making explicit, defensible trade-offs
Because most NFR categories are not actually important in practice
Because Salesforce only allows one NFR category to be prioritized per org
Because functional requirements always take priority over every NFR
questions.explain: NFRs aren't independent dials that can all be turned to maximum — they compete for the same budget, so the architect's real job is making the inevitable trade-offs explicit and agreed-to rather than letting them happen by accident.

questions.q: In the security-vs-performance conflict pair, why can detailed audit logging threaten a performance NFR?
options: Because audit logging is impossible to implement on the Salesforce platform
Because audit logging always runs in a separate Salesforce org
Because logging every field access adds processing overhead to a transaction, which can push response time past a tight performance target under load
Because audit logging disables all governor limits for that transaction
questions.explain: Comprehensive audit logging adds real processing overhead to a transaction. A security NFR demanding that overhead can directly conflict with a tight response-time performance target, especially under peak load.

questions.q: Why are compliance NFRs described as usually the least negotiable when conflicts arise?
options: Because compliance NFRs are always the cheapest to implement

Because they typically carry legal or contractual consequences the business has already accepted, so when they conflict with cost, timeline, or performance, it's usually those other factors that bend instead
Because compliance NFRs never actually conflict with any other NFR category
Because compliance is enforced automatically by Salesforce and requires no trade-off
questions.explain: As established in Lesson 7, compliance NFRs stem from obligations the business has already accepted and generally aren't optional the way a performance target might be — so when a conflict arises, the budget, timeline, or another NFR is more often what gives way.

questions.q: What does this lesson suggest as a better first move than simply picking a side when two NFRs conflict?
options: Escalating immediately to executive leadership without further analysis
Always choosing performance over every other NFR category by default
Deleting whichever NFR is harder to satisfy
Looking for a design change that reduces the conflict itself — such as moving logging to an asynchronous path rather than blocking the synchronous transaction it would otherwise slow down
questions.explain: Before accepting a straight trade-off, it's worth checking whether a design change — like moving audit logging off the synchronous path — can satisfy both NFRs more fully than simply picking one over the other.

questions.q: Why does this lesson treat a team's response of "we'll just do all of it fully" to a named NFR conflict as a warning sign?
options: Because it often signals the conflict hasn't actually been engaged with — either the real cost wasn't estimated, or the conflict was resolved by assumption rather than analysis, instead of ending in a specific, bounded decision
Because doing all of it fully is always technically impossible on Salesforce
Because Salesforce governor limits make this response illegal
Because this response always indicates a compliance violation
questions.explain: A genuine trade-off conversation ends with a specific, bounded decision about what bends and by how much. An unbounded commitment to fully satisfying every conflicting NFR usually means the actual cost and trade-off were never seriously analyzed.
